section.p: This guide is a comprehensive reference for the top-level nginx global object that is available in every JavaScript context created by the JS module. It covers all properties and methods directly on nginx.* — from read-only version information to cross-process coordination primitives — plus the two sub-namespaces nginx.cycle and nginx.events that expose core and event-loop configuration.
Related guides for the deeper sub-namespaces:
Guide 6 (HTTP) [js-reconfig-guide-http.adoc] — nginx.http.*
Guide 5 (Servers) [js-reconfig-guide-servers.adoc] — HTTP server API
Guide 4 (Locations) [js-reconfig-guide-locations.adoc] — HTTP location API
Guide 2 (All Workers) [js-reconfig-guide-all-workers.adoc] — cross-worker coordination
Guide 3 (Checkpoint/Restore) [js-reconfig-guide-checkpoint.adoc] — snapshot API

section.p: nginx.version — the nginx version string as compiled in, e.g. "1.27.3".
nginx.cpu_count — the number of logical CPUs detected by nginx at startup (the value of ngx_ncpu). Useful for setting nginx.cycle.workers to an appropriate value.

stanza.v: // Ensure workers = CPU count at startup

section.p: Writes a message to the nginx error log at the given log level.

: nginx.log is available in all contexts: config phase (js_source), worker request handlers, SharedWorker threads, and JS Worker threads.
The nginx.cycle object exposes the ngx_cycle_t structure — the central nginx process context. It is available in all JS contexts.

nginx.cycle.workers is the only writable cycle property. Write it during config phase (in a js_source script) to adjust the worker count before nginx forks. This is equivalent to the worker_processes directive.

stanza.v: // Auto-size to CPU count (mirrors worker_processes auto;)

section.p: : Writing workers after the fork has no effect on the running process count. Use it only in config-phase scripts.

The nginx.events object exposes the events {} block configuration.
Property │ Type │ R/W │ Description

section.p: : multiAccept and acceptMutex are read by the event loop at worker start. Changing them post-fork has no effect on accepted connections but will be visible to future reads of the property.

section.p: Registers a function to be called in every nginx worker process.
The behaviour differs depending on where broadcast is called:
Context │ Behaviour

Config phase (js_source top-level code, master process) │ fn is appended to the internal nginx.__broadcast_queue. After the master forks, each worker calls every queued function during init_process, with the worker context already set. This lets you register per-worker startup logic that requires worker-only APIs (e.g. nginx.setTimeout, request-level COM objects).
Worker request handler (post-fork) │ fn is called immediately in the current worker only. No IPC to other workers is performed.

stanza.v: │ appended to calls fn() in Worker 1

section.p: : Functions queued via broadcast() in config phase share the same JS runtime and context as the main js_source code. They can close over module-level variables defined in the same script.
Suspends the current async request handler for ms milliseconds using nginx’s event-loop timer infrastructure.
Creates a native ngx_event_t timer in the worker’s event loop.
Returns a Promise that resolves when the timer fires.
While suspended, the worker’s event loop continues processing other connections and timers normally.
After the promise resolves, microtasks are drained and any suspended nginx requests (awaiting the same timer) are finalized.

stanza.v: │ │ worker event loop runs (other requests served)

section.p: setTimeout requires a worker context opaque (set after fork). Calling it from config-phase top-level code throws an error. Use nginx.broadcast to defer setTimeout calls to worker startup:
Per-worker acceptance control (Phase 1). These are synchronous, instant, and affect only the calling worker.

suspendAcceptance() — removes all listening socket read events from this worker’s event loop. Incoming TCP connections continue to queue in the OS SYN backlog (up to net.core.somaxconn) and will be accepted once resumeAcceptance() is called. Other workers continue accepting normally.
resumeAcceptance() — re-adds the listening socket read events. No-op if acceptance was not suspended.
Both functions are only callable from a worker process. Calling from config phase throws a TypeError.

Wrap a batch of COM mutations that must appear atomic from new connections' perspective. Without suspension, a new connection could arrive between two mutations and observe a partially-updated configuration:

stanza.v: // Both mutations applied before any new connection is accepted
(queued conns now accepted with updated config)

section.p: : Because this is per-worker, parallel workers may accept connections with the old config while this worker is suspended. For cluster-wide atomicity use suspendAllWorkers() instead.
Cross-worker acceptance control (Phase 2). Asynchronous; coordinates through the manager process.
Both functions return a Promise that resolves after every worker in the nginx pool has acknowledged the suspend/resume command.
Protocol:

stanza.v: │ └─ reply_fd read event fires → resolve Promise

section.p: If not all workers ack within 500 ms the manager resolves anyway so the calling worker is not stuck. Slow workers will resume acceptance on their own when the next resumeAllWorkers broadcast arrives.

section.p: : Worker 0 is also suspended during this window (it cannot accept new connections). In-flight requests on Worker 0 continue executing.
Creates a TCP listening socket. See Guide 6 [js-reconfig-guide-http.adoc] for the full NginxSocket API and the Phase A-D provisioning pipeline.
Phase │ Context │ Behaviour
A (pre-fork) │ Config phase (js_source top-level code) │ Calls socket() + bind() + listen() directly in the master. All workers inherit the fd on fork.

F (post-fork) │ Worker request handler │ Sends the bind address to the manager thread via AF_UNIX + SCM_RIGHTS. The manager creates the socket and returns the fd to the requesting worker. Use sock.broadcast() to share it with sibling workers.
Two writable properties that configure per-worker resource limits. They are read by init_process (after fork) and cannot be changed at runtime.
Caps the QuickJS heap size for each worker’s JS runtime. After fork, init_process calls JS_SetMemoryLimit(rt, workerMemoryLimit) if the value is non-zero.

stanza.v: // Limit each worker to 128 MB of JS heap

section.p: Caps the wall-clock time a single JS request handler invocation may run. After fork, init_process installs a QuickJS interrupt handler that checks a monotonic-clock deadline set around each JS_Call in the content handler. If the deadline passes, the interrupt handler throws a SyntaxError to terminate the runaway script.

stanza.v: // Kill any request handler that runs for more than 5 seconds

section.p: : The timeout applies to synchronous execution time within a single JS_Call invocation. Async handlers that await nginx.setTimeout() are not penalised for the wall-clock time spent waiting; the deadline is reset at each resume.

workers is the only writable NginxCycle property because it modifies the worker_processes field in ngx_core_conf_t — a plain integer read at fork time. All other cycle fields are either structural (memory pool layouts, allocated arrays) or already computed at config parse time in ways that cannot be safely changed after-the-fact.

JavaScript code evaluated at config phase (inside js_source) runs in the master process before any workers fork. Functions in __broadcast_queue are stored as JS values in the shared context. Because workers inherit the JS runtime via copy-on-write after fork, the queue is accessible in all workers. init_process iterates the queue and calls each function with the worker context opaque already installed, so nginx.setTimeout and request-level COM objects work correctly inside broadcast callbacks.

withSuspendedAcceptance is not a C function — it is a short async function defined in a script string evaluated during ngx_js_com_init. This makes it easy to inspect or override: nginx.withSuspendedAcceptance can be reassigned from JS code for testing purposes.

The timeout is implemented with JS_SetInterruptHandler. Before each JS_Call into a request handler, the C layer records clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) + workerRequestTimeout as a deadline. The interrupt handler fires periodically (QuickJS checks at branch-back points) and compares the current time to the deadline. If exceeded it returns 1, which causes QuickJS to throw a SyntaxError("Script interrupted"). Async suspend points (await) do not advance the deadline; the deadline is re-stamped each time the event loop resumes the handler from a timer or I/O event.
